Flood Insurance Data

Methodology

What we downloaded

We do not use FEMA's summary tables. For every state page we download every NFIP policy record in force and every NFIP claim record FEMA publishes for that state, check the count against the API's own record total (a page is blocked if any record is missing), and compute every figure ourselves. So far: 3,490,299 policy records and 2,680,429 claim records. Each page states its own counts and offers its figures as a CSV.

Sources

  • NFIP Redacted Policies v3 and Claims v3 — OpenFEMA API (keyless). Cost, full-risk premium, zones, claims.
  • Community Status Book v1 — OpenFEMA. CRS class and premium discount by community.
  • Disaster Declarations Summaries v2 — OpenFEMA. Federal flood/storm declarations.
  • Housing Assistance (Owners) v2 — OpenFEMA. FEMA aid paid to owners after disasters.
  • NOAA Sea Level Trends — NOAA Tides & Currents (tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/sltrends). NOAA's own published trend per tide station, in inches per decade with its period; county pages show only a gauge inside the county, never one from another county.
  • National Risk Index (counties) — FEMA ArcGIS (FEMA_NationalRiskIndex). Flood expected annual loss + percentile.
  • Multiple-Loss Flood Properties — OpenFEMA (Individual Assistance). One record per property per declared disaster that damaged it, for properties that flooded more than once; FEMA's disaster-aid data flags some as severe repeat-loss (SRL).
  • Official Policy Information by State and Community workbook — listed for reference; the pages are not yet checked against it.

Eight federal datasets; the full-risk premium is a field within Policies and the PIF workbook is a reference, not a separate fetch. Each page lists the ones it uses.

Definitions & rules

  • Policy units = sum of policyCount, never a row count — condo-association records carry more than one unit.
  • Cost cohort: single-family primary-residence policies (occupancy 1/11, primary residence), annual cost = premium + fees.
  • Percentiles p25/p50/p75/p90 by inclusive interpolation.
  • Full-risk gap: share of cohort whose premium charged (totalInsurancePremiumOfThePolicy) is below FEMA's full-risk premium (fullRiskPremium); both are premium-only. The cost figures elsewhere use policyCost, which FEMA defines as premium plus the reserve fund assessment, federal policy fee and HFIAA surcharge, so they are not compared with full-risk.
  • Claims against policies: cumulative claims since 1978 beside current policy units — a historical tally, not an annual rate or a flood probability.
  • Minimum sizes: a cost spread needs 100 or more priced single-family policies; a flood-zone median 50; a county median 30; a ZIP median 25. Smaller medians move more from year to year, and the count is shown beside each.
  • Dates: each figure shows its effective date and retrieval date; policy snapshot differs from other datasets' retrieval dates.

What the data cannot tell you

  • Your own premium: it depends on your building's elevation, foundation, coverage and deductible. The pages show where existing policies fall, and what policies first bought in the past year typically cost.
  • Private (non-NFIP) flood insurance prices.
  • Your address's exact flood zone: use FEMA's Flood Map Service Center.
  • Why any one premium changes: the pages show the gap to FEMA's full-risk price, not the cause.
  • A long premium trend: the in-force records hold only current-term policies, so only the last two policy years can be compared.

How each figure is counted

Policy units by flood zone

Insured units by the flood zone each policy is rated in; a condo-building policy counts each of its units.

ZIP codes

A ZIP median is shown when the ZIP has 25 or more priced single-family policies; otherwise the lookup gives its policy count. Policy units also count condo units, so they can be far more than the priced policies. Each town name is the Census place with the largest share of that ZIP code area.

Why published prices differ

Published figures rarely say which measure they are, or which year. Policies renew on their own anniversaries, so the latest term year shows where renewals are heading. Private flood insurance is not in FEMA's data.

Rebuilding cost and the building limit

Rebuilding cost is the replacement-cost figure on single-family primary-home policies that report one. Many owners insure to the building maximum even when that figure is lower, so the two shares measure different things. The damage share counts every paid claim with a damage figure, all building types.

Claims closed without payment

The building non-payment reason on each NFIP claim closed with nothing paid, every claim counted once. “Assigned in error” and “Other” are FEMA's own labels; some closed claims are paperwork, not a denied flood.

Flood events

Paid NFIP claims grouped by the flood event FEMA assigned (FEMA's name). A catch-all label spanning many years gets its own row; floods with too few paid claims here to count as one flood (see the card) are not listed. Event totals include code-upgrade (ICC) payments, which the yearly totals leave out.

Claims by year

Net building and contents payments by year of loss. Claims are matched by the claims dataset's county code, which may not exactly match a policy's property county.

Repeat-flood records

One home appears once for each declared disaster that damaged it, so the count is damage events on repeat-flooded homes, not distinct homes (FEMA says these records cannot be totaled by property). Disaster-aid records since 2002, separate from NFIP insurance claims.

Disaster declarations

Distinct storms by calendar year: one storm's emergency and major-disaster declarations are counted once, not each declaration record.

FEMA's National Risk Index

The rating is FEMA's modeled expected flood loss, adjusted for social vulnerability and community resilience, compared across counties (coastal and inland flooding are rated separately). Because it weighs vulnerability and resilience, and a place with many valuable buildings can have a large total loss but a low loss per dollar, the rating and the loss percentile can differ. Any loss figure is a whole-county model of all flood loss, insured or not, averaged per year, so it runs far above insurance payouts; it is never one home's expected loss or premium.
